meiosis-s1.title: DNA content of one cell through meiosis
meiosis-s1.html:
In a lily flower, cells inside the anther (the part that makes pollen) divide by meiosis. Lily body cells have 2n = 24. Researchers measured the DNA content of one such cell every 2 hours, starting in G1, using a dye whose brightness is proportional to DNA. After each division they followed one of the new cells. DNA content is in relative units, with the cell in G1 set at 2.

meiosis-s2.title: Four dividing cells from one plant
meiosis-s2.html:
A student looked at stained cells from a plant whose body cells have 2n = 6: two long, two medium and two short chromosomes. She described four cells, W to Z, from different parts of the plant. All four were stopped while their chromosomes were condensed.

meiosis-genetic-diversity-s1.title: Mother's age and births with trisomy 21
meiosis-genetic-diversity-s1.html:
The table gives approximate rates of births with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) by the mother's age at delivery, pooled from large population surveys. Family studies of DNA show that in about 90% of cases the extra chromosome 21 came from the egg, and that most of those egg errors happened in meiosis I. Human egg cells begin meiosis I before the mother herself is born and stay paused partway through prophase I, with homologs paired, until shortly before that egg is released, which can be 12 to 50 years later.

meiosis-genetic-diversity-s2.title: Tracing an extra chromosome 21
meiosis-genetic-diversity-s2.html:
The karyotype is from child A. To find where the extra chromosome came from, researchers read a stretch of DNA close to the centromere of chromosome 21. This stretch comes in many slightly different types, numbered here; each copy of chromosome 21 carries one type. Crossing over almost never happens this close to the centromere. They tested child A and the parents, and also a child with the same karyotype from another family, child B.

Types of the DNA stretch found on chromosome 21 in each person
PersonTypes found
Child A's father1 and 2
Child A's mother3 and 4
Child A1, 3 and 4
Child B's father5 and 6
Child B's mother7 and 8
Child B5, 6 and 8

mendelian-genetics-s1.title: A family with a rare trait
mendelian-genetics-s1.html: The pedigree shows three generations of a family in which some members have a rare condition caused by one gene. II-4 married into the family and has no relatives with the condition. Use A for the allele that does not cause the condition and a for the allele that does.

mendelian-genetics-s2.title: Kernels on an ear of corn
mendelian-genetics-s2.html:
Each kernel on an ear of corn is a seed, the offspring of one fertilization. A true-breeding plant grown from purple, smooth kernels was crossed with a true-breeding plant grown from yellow, wrinkled kernels. Every F1 kernel was purple and smooth. F1 plants were then self-pollinated, and students counted the F2 kernels on one ear. Kernel color and kernel texture are each controlled by one gene, on different chromosome pairs.

F2 kernels on one ear, by color and texture

non-mendelian-genetics-s1.title: Offspring counts from a fruit fly testcross
non-mendelian-genetics-s1.html:
A true-breeding gray-bodied, red-eyed fly was crossed with a true-breeding black-bodied, purple-eyed fly. Gray (B) is dominant to black (b) and red (P) to purple (p). An F1 female (BbPp) was then crossed with a black, purple-eyed male (bbpp), and the offspring were counted.

non-mendelian-genetics-s2.title: Coat colors of Labrador retriever puppies
non-mendelian-genetics-s2.html:
In Labrador retrievers, gene B controls the dark pigment made in hair: B (black) is dominant to b (brown, called chocolate). A second gene, E, on another chromosome, controls whether that pigment is put into the hair at all: dogs with genotype ee cannot deposit it and are yellow. A breeder pooled the litters of several matings between dogs that were all BbEe.

Puppies from BbEe × BbEe matings

Yellow39

non-mendelian-genetics-s3.title: Leaf color in four o'clock plants
non-mendelian-genetics-s3.html:
Some four o'clock plants have branches of three kinds: green, white (no working chloroplasts), and variegated (patches of green and white). Each flower makes both eggs and pollen, and the plant has no sex chromosomes. A botanist moved pollen from flowers on one kind of branch onto flowers on another kind, then grew the seeds.

environment-phenotype-s1.title: Hydrangea clones in soils of different pH
environment-phenotype-s1.html:
A grower took 48 cuttings from one hydrangea plant and rooted them in pots. Groups of 8 were grown in the same potting mix adjusted to six different pH values, with the same light, water and temperature. When the plants flowered, she recorded each plant's flower color and measured aluminum in the colored flower parts (4 plants per group).

Eggs from 10 nests of one turtle species were collected, and the eggs of each nest were divided among seven incubators held at 26 to 32 °C, so every incubator received eggs from every nest. items.q: During which interval is the cell copying its DNA?
options: From 4 to 10 hours
From 20 to 22 hours
From 26 to 28 hours
From 10 to 20 hours

items.q: A cell at 2 hours and a cell at 24 hours both have a DNA content of 2. How do their chromosomes differ?
options: At 24 hours: 12 chromosomes of two chromatids each. At 2 hours: 24 chromosomes of one chromatid each.
At 24 hours: 24 chromosomes of two chromatids each. At 2 hours: 12 chromosomes of one chromatid each.
They do not differ: cells with the same DNA content have the same number and kind of chromosomes.
At 24 hours: 12 chromosomes of one chromatid each. At 2 hours: 24 chromosomes of two chromatids each.

items.q: How many sister chromatids does the cell contain at 16 hours? Give a whole number.

In a second experiment, a drug that stops spindle fibers from forming was added at 12 hours. The cells stayed alive, did not divide and did not copy their DNA again. Predict the DNA content of a cell at 30 hours.
options: 4 units
2 units
1 unit
8 units

items.q: Between 26 and 28 hours the DNA content per cell halves, from 2 to 1, yet the number of chromosomes per cell does not change. Which explanation fits?
options: Sister chromatids separate into different cells, and no S phase came between the two divisions.
Homologous chromosomes separate into different cells for a second time.
Half of the DNA in each chromosome is broken down after the first division.
The cell copies its DNA again and then divides into four cells at once.

items.q: Which cell is in metaphase of meiosis I?
options: Cell X
Cell W
Cell Y
Cell Z

items.q: Cells W and Y both have chromosomes lined up singly across the middle. Which observation shows that Y is in meiosis II rather than mitosis?
options: Y holds one chromosome of each length, so the homologs have already been separated.
Each of Y's chromosomes is made of two sister chromatids.
Y's chromosomes are lined up in one row across the middle of the cell.
Y has fewer chromosomes because three were broken down during meiosis I.

items.q: How many chromatids are in cell X in total? Give a whole number.
Select the cells that are haploid.
options: Cell W
Cell X
Cell Y
Cell Z

items.q: Cell Y completes its division. Predict what each of the resulting cells contains.
options: 3 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
3 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
6 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
1 or 2 chromosomes, as an odd number does not split evenly

items.q: A dog's skin cells have 78 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a dog sperm cell have? Give a whole number.
In a man's liver cell in G2, a biologist compares the two copies of chromosome 7 with each other, and the two sister chromatids of one copy with each other. Which statement is correct?
options: The sister chromatids carry identical DNA; the two chromosome 7s have the same genes but may carry different alleles.
The two chromosome 7s carry identical DNA, because they are copies of the same chromosome.
The two sister chromatids came from different parents, one from his mother and one from his father.
The two chromosome 7s carry different genes, one set inherited from each of his parents.

items.q: Suppose a plant with 2n = 14 made its sperm and egg cells by mitosis instead of meiosis. What would its offspring's chromosome number be, and why?
options: 28, because two gametes with 14 chromosomes each would join
14, because mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same
7, because each gamete would carry half of the 14
14, because fertilization would halve the number again

items.q: In the human life cycle, which event turns haploid cells into a diploid cell?
options: Fertilization
Meiosis I
Meiosis II
Mitosis in the zygote

items.q: Compare a sperm cell made by a man's meiosis with one of his skin cells in G1. For the sperm cell, predict whether each value is higher (up), lower (down) or the same (no change).

variables.name: Number of chromosomes
Amount of DNA in the nucleus
Number of different kinds of autosome (each kind counted once)
Number of copies of chromosome 1

items.q: Put the events of meiosis in order, starting before meiosis begins.
options: DNA is copied, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids.
Homologous chromosomes pair along their length.
Pairs of homologs line up side by side across the middle of the cell.
The homologs of each pair move to opposite poles and the cell divides in two.
In each new cell, chromosomes line up singly across the middle.
Sister chromatids separate, giving four haploid cells.

items.q: A karyotype shows 22 pairs of autosomes plus one X and one Y chromosome. Which cell could it have come from?
options: A skin cell of a male
A sperm cell of a male
A skin cell of a female
An egg cell of a female

items.q: Select the statements that are true of both meiosis II and mitosis.
options: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
Chromosomes line up singly across the middle of the cell.
Homologous chromosomes pair before lining up.
The division begins straight after an S phase.
The division turns a diploid cell into haploid cells.

items.q: A mule has 63 chromosomes: 32 from its horse mother and 31 from its donkey father. Mules grow normally but almost never make working gametes. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Horse and donkey chromosomes differ, so many fail to pair as homologs in meiosis I and are shared out unevenly.
An odd number of chromosomes is not copied properly in S phase, so the mule's cells stop dividing.
Mule body cells divide by meiosis instead of mitosis, so they become haploid before the mule matures.
Mule body cells fail to divide by mitosis, because 63 chromosomes do not split equally into two cells.

items.q: Male honeybees develop from unfertilized eggs and have 16 chromosomes; females develop from fertilized eggs and have 32. Males make sperm by a division that does not halve the chromosome number. How many chromosomes does a male's sperm carry, and why does the female number stay at 32?
options: 16; the male is already haploid, so a 16-chromosome sperm and a 16-chromosome egg give 32.
8; sperm are made by halving, so a 16-chromosome egg and an 8-chromosome sperm give 24.
32; the sperm doubles the male's number, so it matches the female number by itself.
16; the sperm carries the queen's chromosomes, which it received when the male was fertilized.

items.q: Corn has 2n = 20. How many tetrads (pairs of homologous chromosomes) line up across the middle of a corn cell in metaphase of meiosis I? Give a whole number.
How many times higher is the rate of births with trisomy 21 for mothers aged 45 than for mothers aged 25? Give a whole number.
Which statement best describes the pattern in the table?
options: The rate rises slowly from 20 to 30 years and much more steeply after 35.
The rate rises by about the same number of births per 10,000 in each five-year step.
The rate doubles in each five-year step from 20 to 45 years.
The rate is nearly flat until 40 and then rises in one sudden step.

items.q: Which hypothesis best explains both the age pattern and the finding that most extra chromosomes come from meiosis I in the egg?
options: Links holding each paused homolog pair together weaken with time, so a pair more often goes to one pole.
Eggs of older women copy chromosome 21 twice in S phase, so the egg enters meiosis I with an extra copy of it.
Older mothers usually have older partners, whose sperm more often carry two copies of chromosome 21 after meiosis.
In older mothers the embryo's body cells divide less accurately by mitosis, adding a chromosome 21 after fertilization.

items.q: A large hospital records 4,000 births to mothers aged 40. Using the table, how many of these births would you expect to have trisomy 21? Give a whole number.
A student concludes from the table that the father's age is the main cause of the rise in trisomy 21. Which response is best supported by the information given?
options: The data group births by the mother's age, and most extra copies come from eggs, so they point to her age.
The conclusion is supported, because sperm are made throughout a man's life, so older men's sperm carry more errors.
The conclusion is supported, because the rate rises with age in the table, and both parents grow older together.
The table says nothing about either parent's age, because trisomy 21 is caused by crossing over in meiosis.

items.q: How many chromosomes are in each body cell of child A? Give a whole number.
Which gamete that formed child A was abnormal, and how many chromosomes did it carry?
options: The egg, with 24 chromosomes
The sperm, with 24 chromosomes
The egg, with 22 chromosomes
Neither; both carried 23, and a chromosome 21 was copied after fertilization

items.q: In which division did the error that produced child A most likely occur?
options: Meiosis I in the mother, because the egg carried both of her different chromosome 21s
Meiosis II in the mother, because the egg carried both of her different chromosome 21s
Meiosis I in the father, because the child carries one of his two types
Mitosis in the early embryo, because the child has three copies in each cell

items.q: Child B's types (5, 6 and 8) show that the extra chromosome came from a meiosis I error in the father. What else was true of the other three sperm cells made from that same cell's meiosis?
options: One more carried two chromosome 21s, and two carried no chromosome 21.
The other three were normal, with one chromosome 21 each.
One carried no chromosome 21, and the other two were normal.
The other three each carried two copies of chromosome 21.

items.q: Why did the researchers read a DNA stretch close to the centromere rather than one near the tip of chromosome 21?
options: Crossing over rarely reaches there, so the type shows which parental homolog each copy came from.
DNA near the centromere is copied in S phase, while the DNA near the tips is left uncopied.
Sister chromatids differ near the centromere, which lets the two kinds of error be told apart.
The region near the centromere is passed on to children, while the tips of the chromosome stay in the parent.

items.q: A fruit fly has 2n = 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of chromosomes can its gametes receive by independent assortment? Give a whole number.

A species has 2n = 6, and each parent's two homologs of every pair differ. Ignoring crossing over, how many different chromosome combinations could one pair of parents produce in their offspring? Give a whole number.
Select the process that can put alleles from both of a parent's homologs onto one chromosome in a gamete.
options: Crossing over in prophase I
Independent assortment at metaphase I
Random fertilization
Separation of sister chromatids in anaphase II
Copying of DNA in S phase

items.q: A plant has identical alleles on the two homologs of every pair, at every gene. Its pollen fertilizes its own eggs. Predict how the offspring compare with the parent and with each other.
options: Identical to the parent and to each other, since meiosis just reshuffles alleles that are the same.
They differ from one another, because crossing over makes new combinations of alleles in each meiosis.
They differ, because independent assortment gives 2ⁿ different gametes in any plant.
They have half the parent's chromosome number, because just one parent was involved.

items.q: Put these sources of variety in the order in which they happen in one generation.
options: Paired homologs swap pieces of chromatid (crossing over).
Homologous pairs line up at the middle, each either way round (independent assortment).
Sister chromatids separate into four haploid cells.
A sperm fuses with an egg (random fertilization).

items.q: A diploid yeast cell divides by meiosis to make four haploid spores. A mutant strain pairs its homologs normally but makes no crossovers; assume its chromosomes still separate correctly. Compared with normal yeast, predict each value for the mutant.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in each spore
Number of different allele combinations among spores from many cells
Fraction of spores with a chromosome carrying alleles from both homologs
Number of whole-chromosome combinations possible from independent assortment

items.q: A girl's karyotype shows 45 chromosomes, with a single X and no other sex chromosome (Turner syndrome). Which pair of gametes could have produced her?
options: A normal egg with an X, and a sperm with no sex chromosome
An egg with two X chromosomes, and a normal sperm with a Y
A normal egg with an X, and a normal sperm with an X
An egg with no sex chromosome, and a normal sperm with a Y

items.q: Most cases of Down syndrome are caused by
options: three copies of chromosome 21 in each cell
a single copy of chromosome 21 in each body cell
a missing X chromosome in each body cell
an extra Y chromosome in each cell

items.q: In a cell with 2n = 8, one homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I; meiosis II is normal. How many chromosomes do the four gametes have?
A boy has 47 chromosomes with XXY (Klinefelter syndrome). DNA tests show one X came from his mother and the other X and the Y came from his father. In which division did the error happen?
options: Meiosis I in the father: the X and Y, which pair in meiosis I, went into the same sperm.
Meiosis II in the father: the two X chromatids failed to separate, giving an XX sperm.
Meiosis I in the mother: her two X chromosomes failed to separate and went into one egg.
Meiosis II in the mother: her X chromatids went into the same egg.

items.q: Ignoring crossing over, what is the chance that two children of the same mother receive exactly the same set of chromosomes from her?
options: About 1 in 8.4 million
About 1 in 23 (one chance per pair)
About 1 in 46 (one per chromosome)
About 1 in 2, the chance for one pair

items.q: A new fungus kills a crop plant unless the plant has a rare combination of alleles at several genes. Farm 1 grows plants all made from cuttings of one plant (by mitosis); farm 2 grows plants from seeds made by sexual reproduction. Which farm is more likely to have surviving plants, and why?
options: Farm 2, because meiosis and fertilization give each seedling a different allele combination.
Farm 1, because plants made by mitosis keep both full chromosome sets of a single healthy parent.
Farm 2, because sexual reproduction invents alleles in response to the fungus.
Both equally, because plants of one species carry the same genes.

items.q: Which mode of inheritance is most consistent with the pedigree, and which individual's phenotype rules out X-linked recessive inheritance?
options: Autosomal recessive; III-1 is an affected daughter of an unaffected father, II-4.
Autosomal dominant; II-1 is affected even though both of his parents are unaffected.
X-linked recessive; II-1, an affected son, has a mother who does not show the trait.
Autosomal recessive; II-1 is an affected son of an unaffected mother, I-2.

items.q: Select every individual who must be heterozygous (Aa).
options: II-2
II-3
II-4
III-3

items.q: What is the probability that II-2 is a carrier (Aa)? Give a decimal to two places.
II-3 and II-4 plan another child. What is the probability that the child is a boy with the condition? Give a decimal to three places.
III-3 has a child with a man who has the condition. What is the probability that this child has the condition? Give a decimal to two places.
Which alleles are dominant?
options: The purple allele and the smooth allele
The yellow allele and the wrinkled allele
The purple allele and the wrinkled allele
The yellow allele and the smooth allele

items.q: Considering color alone, calculate the ratio of purple to yellow F2 kernels, as the number of purple kernels per yellow kernel. Give one decimal place.
If the two genes assort independently, how many of the 390 F2 kernels would you predict to be yellow and wrinkled? Give a whole number.
The F2 counts are close to a 9:3:3:1 ratio. Which explanation connects that ratio to events in the F1 plants' meiosis?
options: The two genes' chromosome pairs line up independently at metaphase I, so PS, Ps, pS and ps gametes form in equal numbers and combine at random.
Homologs pair and swap pieces in each meiosis, which makes the four kernel types appear in a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
The purple and smooth alleles are dominant, so they go into 9 out of 16 gametes and the recessive alleles into the rest.
Each F1 plant makes two kinds of gamete, PS and ps, and their random combination at fertilization gives 9:3:3:1.

items.q: A student grows a plant from one purple, smooth F2 kernel and wants to know its genotype. Which cross and result would show that it is PpSs?
options: Cross it with a plant from a yellow, wrinkled kernel; find the four phenotypes in about equal numbers.
Cross it with a plant from a purple, smooth kernel; find purple, smooth offspring and no other kind.
Cross it with a plant from a yellow, wrinkled kernel; find purple, smooth offspring and no others.
Self-pollinate it; find purple, smooth and yellow, wrinkled kernels in a 3:1 ratio.

items.q: Two plants with genotype AaBbCc are crossed; the three genes assort independently. The chance that an offspring is aabbcc is 1 in how many? Give a whole number.
In a cross AaBb × Aabb (genes on different chromosome pairs; A and B dominant), what proportion of offspring are expected to show both dominant traits? Give a decimal to three places.
Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive condition. What is the probability that their next child neither has cystic fibrosis nor is a carrier?
In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to white (b). A black guinea pig is crossed with a white one, and the litters include 7 black and 6 white offspring. What is the black parent's genotype?
options: Bb, heterozygous
BB, homozygous dominant
bb, homozygous recessive
Unknown, since BB and Bb both look black

items.q: Red-green color blindness is X-linked recessive. A color-blind man has children with a woman who has normal vision but whose father was color-blind. What is expected among their children?
options: Half of their sons and half of their daughters are color-blind.
Half of their sons are color-blind, and their daughters have normal vision.
Their sons have normal vision, and half of their daughters are color-blind.
One quarter of their children are color-blind, and those are sons.

items.q: Why are X-linked recessive conditions such as hemophilia much more common in males than in females?
options: A male's single X has no partner, so one recessive allele shows; a female needs two.
The Y chromosome carries a dominant allele that switches the condition on in males.
Males inherit their X chromosome from their father, who is more likely to carry the allele.
Recessive alleles on the X are copied more often during meiosis in males than in females.

items.q: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant, and symptoms usually begin between ages 30 and 50. A man develops it at 45; his mother was never affected and lived to 85. His 20-year-old daughter has no symptoms, and her mother has no family history of the disease. What is the probability that she carries the Huntington's allele?
options: 0, because she has no symptoms
1, because her father is affected

items.q: Which event in meiosis is the physical basis of the law of segregation?
options: Homologs separate in anaphase I, so each gamete gets one allele of each gene.
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II, so each gamete gets two identical alleles.
Homologs swap pieces in prophase I, so alleles move between chromosomes.
DNA is copied before meiosis, so each allele is present twice.

items.q: Select the condition that, by itself, makes two genes assort independently in Mendel's sense.
options: The two genes are on different chromosome pairs.
Each gene has one dominant and one recessive allele.
The two genes affect related traits, such as seed color and seed coat color.
The parents in the P generation are true-breeding.
The F1 plants are self-pollinated rather than crossed with each other.

items.q: Segregation and independent assortment explain inheritance in peas, fruit flies, yeast and humans, and all of these use DNA in chromosomes that are shared out by meiosis. What do these shared mechanisms most strongly suggest?
options: They share common ancestry and inherited the same machinery from it.
Each group evolved its own meiosis that happens to follow the same rules.
Pea plants were the first organisms, and the other groups descend from them.
Mendel's laws apply to plants, and animals copy them by learning.

items.q: Put the steps of a monohybrid experiment like Mendel's in order.
options: Grow plants that are true-breeding for each form of the trait.
Cross the two true-breeding types (P generation).
Record that every F1 plant shows one form of the trait.
Self-pollinate the F1 plants.
Count the F2 plants of each form and find a ratio near 3:1.

items.q: In fruit flies, white eyes (w) is X-linked recessive to red eyes. Cross 1: a red-eyed (homozygous) female × a white-eyed male. Cross 2: a white-eyed female × a red-eyed male. Compared with cross 1, predict each value for the offspring of cross 2.

variables.name: Fraction of sons with white eyes
Fraction of daughters with white eyes
Fraction of daughters who carry the white allele
Fraction of all offspring with red eyes

items.q: Which offspring classes are recombinant?
options: Gray with purple eyes, and black with red eyes
Gray with red eyes, and black with purple eyes
Gray with red eyes, and gray with purple eyes
Black with purple eyes, and black with red eyes

items.q: Calculate the recombination frequency between the body-color and eye-color genes, in percent. Give one decimal place.
If the two genes assorted independently, how many flies would be expected in each of the four classes? Give a whole number.
A chi-square test of the counts against the 1:1:1:1 ratio gives χ² ≈ 760. Which conclusion is correct?
options: With 3 degrees of freedom the critical value is 7.82, so reject independent assortment; the genes are likely linked.
With 4 degrees of freedom the critical value is 9.49, so reject independent assortment; the genes are likely linked.
With 3 degrees of freedom the critical value is 7.82, so fail to reject independent assortment.
χ² is far above the critical value, which shows that the genes are on different chromosomes.

items.q: The two recombinant classes are about equal in size (31 and 33), and so are the two parental classes. Which explanation fits?
options: Each crossover between the genes swaps pieces between two chromatids, making one B p and one b P chromatid together.
Gray and black flies survive equally well, so any two classes end up with similar numbers.
Recombinant offspring are made by the male parent, who passes on b p and B P equally.
Crossing over happens in about half of the meioses, so each recombinant class is about half of the total.

items.q: Which genotypes give a yellow coat?
options: Any genotype with ee, whatever the B gene alleles
bbee, the double recessive genotype, and no other
Any genotype with bb, whatever the E gene alleles
Any genotype with Ee, because one E is not enough

items.q: Calculate χ² for the puppy counts against an expected ratio of 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow. Give two decimal places.
Using χ² ≈ 0.10 for the 9:3:4 hypothesis, which conclusion is correct at p = 0.05?
options: df = 2, critical value 5.99; fail to reject, so the counts are consistent with 9:3:4.
df = 3, critical value 7.82; fail to reject, so the counts are consistent with 9:3:4.
df = 2, critical value 5.99; reject, so the counts do not fit 9:3:4.
df = 2, critical value 5.99; this proves the 9:3:4 hypothesis is true.

items.q: A yellow Labrador with genotype BBee is mated with a chocolate Labrador with genotype bbEE. Predict the coat color of their puppies.
options: Black
Yellow
Chocolate
Half yellow and half chocolate

items.q: Why do these matings give a 9:3:4 ratio instead of the 9:3:3:1 of a typical dihybrid cross?
options: The B_ee (3/16) and bbee (1/16) classes are both yellow, so they merge into 4/16.
The two genes are linked, so just three of the four classes appear.
One of the four expected classes, bbee, dies before birth.
Chocolate is incompletely dominant, so B_E_ and bbE_ blend into one class.

items.q: Which pattern do the results show?
options: The seedlings resemble the branch that gave the eggs.
The seedlings resemble the branch that gave the pollen.
Green is dominant, so green seedlings appear in each cross.
The seedlings show a 3:1 ratio of green to white.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the results?
options: The trait depends on chloroplasts, which pass to the seedling in the egg's cytoplasm, not in the pollen.
The trait is caused by a recessive allele in the nucleus, which is hidden when pollen brings a dominant allele.
The trait is X-linked, so it passes from the plant giving the eggs to its offspring.
The pollen's chloroplasts are destroyed by the egg's nucleus at fertilization.

items.q: Rows 2 and 4 are a reciprocal cross. Why does their difference rule out an ordinary nuclear gene?
options: For a nuclear gene, each parent gives one allele, so swapping which branch gives eggs would not change the seedlings.
For a nuclear gene, swapping the parents doubles the number of white seedlings.
Nuclear genes are carried in pollen but not in eggs, so the eggs could not pass them on.
A nuclear gene would give a 9:3:3:1 ratio in both crosses.

items.q: A condition in humans is caused by a change in mitochondrial DNA. Predict the children of family 1 (affected mother, unaffected father) and family 2 (unaffected mother, affected father).
options: Children in family 1 can inherit it; in family 2 the children are very unlikely to.
Children in family 2 can inherit it; in family 1 the children are very unlikely to.
Half the children in each family inherit it, as for a dominant nuclear allele.
Sons in family 1 and daughters in family 2 inherit it, as for an X-linked allele.

items.q: In snapdragons, red (C<sup>R</sup>C<sup>R</sup>) × white (C<sup>W</sup>C<sup>W</sup>) gives pink offspring. What ratio of flower colors is expected when two pink plants are crossed?
options: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
3 pink : 1 white
3 red : 1 white
1 red : 1 white

items.q: A mother has blood type A and her child has type O. Which man can be ruled out as the child's father on blood type alone?
options: A man with type AB
A man with type A
A man with type B
A man with type O

items.q: A man with genotype I<sup>A</sup>i and a woman with genotype I<sup>B</sup>i have a child. What is the probability that the child has blood type AB? Give a decimal to two places.
A red bull and a white cow have a calf whose coat is a mixture of red hairs and white hairs (roan). Which pattern of inheritance does this show, and why?
options: Codominance, because each allele's color appears fully, in separate hairs.
Incomplete dominance, because the calf's coat is a blend of its parents' colors.
Complete dominance, because the calf shows red, which is the dominant color.
Epistasis, because one gene for coat color masks another.

items.q: A plant's height is controlled by three genes (A, B, C) on different chromosomes. Each capital-letter allele adds 2 cm to a base height, and the effects simply add up. How many different heights are possible among the offspring of AaBbCc × AaBbCc? Give a whole number.

The gene that is altered in cystic fibrosis makes a channel protein used in the lungs, pancreas, sweat glands and reproductive tract. People with two altered copies have thick mucus in the lungs, digestive problems, salty sweat and often reduced fertility. This is an example of
options: pleiotropy
epistasis
polygenic inheritance
codominance

items.q: Three genes are on one chromosome. Recombination frequencies are: A–B 12%, B–C 4%, A–C 8%. What is the gene order?
options: A – C – B
A – B – C
B – A – C
C – A – B

items.q: A testcross of AaBb × aabb gives four phenotype classes. Select the result that is evidence that genes A and B are linked.
options: Two classes make up about 90% of the offspring, and the other two about 10%.
The four classes appear in about equal numbers.
The dominant phenotype for each gene appears in about half of the offspring.
About three quarters of the offspring show the dominant phenotype for both genes.
Each offspring shows the dominant phenotype for gene A.

items.q: Gene pair 1 is 5 map units apart on a chromosome; gene pair 2 is 30 map units apart on the same chromosome. In matching testcrosses of double heterozygotes, predict each value for gene pair 2 compared with gene pair 1.

variables.name: Recombination frequency
Percentage of parental-type offspring
Number of phenotype classes among the offspring
Number of chromosomes in each gamete

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship in the table?
options: As soil pH rises, flowers shift from blue to pink and aluminum in the flowers falls.
As soil pH rises, flowers shift from pink to blue and aluminum in the flowers rises.
Flower color changes with pH, but aluminum in the flowers stays about the same.
Aluminum in the flowers falls as pH rises, but flower color does not change.

items.q: Why did the grower use cuttings from one plant instead of seedlings?
options: Cuttings share one genotype, so group differences come from the soil, not genes.
Cuttings grow faster than seedlings, so the plants flower within a single season.
Seedlings rarely flower in pots, so cuttings were the one way to see a flower color.
Cuttings take up more aluminum from soil than seedlings, making the color change larger.

items.q: A student claims that aluminum, not acidity itself, turns the flowers blue. Which additional experiment would best test the claim?
options: At pH 5.0, grow cuttings in soil with aluminum removed or bound and in soil with it, all else equal.
Grow more cuttings at each of the six pH values and measure aluminum in their leaves and roots as well as their flowers.
Grow seedlings instead of cuttings at pH 4.5 and at pH 7.0, then compare the flower colors of the two groups.
Measure the soil pH again at the end of the experiment to check that it stayed steady during the season.

items.q: What percentage of the plants grown at pH 6.0 had blue or purple flowers? Give one decimal place.
Using the ± 2 SE values, which comparison of aluminum in the flowers shows a difference that is likely to be real?
options: pH 5.5 compared with pH 6.0
pH 4.5 compared with pH 5.0
pH 6.5 compared with pH 7.0
Not one of these pairs shows a likely difference

items.q: From the graph, at what incubation temperature do about half of the hatchlings develop as females? Give a whole number of degrees Celsius.
On one beach, nests have been incubating at about 28 °C. If warmer summers raise nest temperatures to about 30 °C, predict the effect on the hatchlings.
options: The share of females rises from about 18% to about 86%.
The share of females falls from about 86% to about 18%.
The sex ratio stays the same, because sex is set by the hatchlings' genes.
Each hatchling becomes female, because warming above 28 °C gives females.

items.q: Why did the researchers divide the eggs of each nest among all seven incubators?
options: So nest-to-nest genetic differences were spread across temperatures, leaving temperature as the one difference.
So that each incubator held the same number of eggs, which made the incubators warm up evenly.
So that eggs from the same mother would hatch as the same sex in each incubator they were placed in.
So that the researchers could later tell which of the ten nests each hatchling came from just by looking at its sex.

items.q: Do the error bars support a real difference in the percentage of females between 31 °C and 32 °C?
options: No; 97 ± 3 reaches 100, so the two intervals overlap.
Yes; 100% is higher than 97%, so the difference is real.
Yes; the error bars at 32 °C are zero, so any difference is real.
No; percentages are not compared using error bars.

items.q: A conservation group incubates 40 eggs at 30 °C. Using the mean in the graph, about how many of the hatchlings should be female? Give a whole number.
A patch of white fur is shaved from the warm back of a Himalayan rabbit, and an ice pack is kept on the patch while the fur grows back. Predict the color of the new fur and the reason.
options: Dark, because the pigment enzyme works in the cooled skin.
White, because the rabbit's genotype for that patch codes for white fur.
White, because shaving damages the hair follicles in that patch.
Dark, because the cold changes the rabbit's alleles in that patch.

items.q: Siamese cats have dark ears, face, paws and tail. Which explanation of this pattern is best?
options: Their pigment enzyme loses its working shape at body-core temperature but works in the cooler extremities.
Cells in the ears and paws carry different alleles for coat color from the cells in the rest of the body.
Dark pigment made in the warm body moves outward through the blood and collects in the extremities.
Cats inherit dark extremities by a second gene, as a separate trait from the color of the body fur.

items.q: A child with PKU (genotype pp) eats a low-phenylalanine diet from birth and develops normally. Which statement is correct?
options: Her genotype is still pp, but the diet changed her phenotype by keeping phenylalanine low.
The diet changed her genotype from pp to Pp, which is why she developed normally.
She does not really have PKU, because PKU by definition causes harm to the brain.
Her children will not inherit PKU alleles from her, because the diet has treated the condition.

items.q: Compare a child with PKU who eats a low-phenylalanine diet from birth with a child with PKU who eats a normal diet. For the child on the low-phenylalanine diet, predict each value.

variables.name: Phenylalanine level in the blood
Number of copies of the PKU allele in each cell
Risk of harm to brain development
Chance of passing a PKU allele to each future child

items.q: Identical twins have the same genotype, yet one twin, raised with poor nutrition, is 8 cm shorter as an adult than the other. What does this show about height?
options: Height is multifactorial: genes set a range, and the environment decides where in it a person lands.
Height is controlled by one gene with two alleles, and the shorter twin received a recessive allele for it.
Height is not affected by genes, because twins with exactly the same genes can still differ in it.
The twins have different genotypes for height, since their adult heights differ by a full 8 cm.

items.q: Clones of two corn varieties were grown in low-nitrogen and high-nitrogen soil. Variety 1 was taller in low-nitrogen soil; variety 2 was taller in high-nitrogen soil. What does this show?
options: Which genotype grows taller depends on the environment: their norms of reaction cross.
Variety 1 has better alleles for height overall, because it is the taller one in poor soil.
Soil nitrogen changes the alleles of each variety, so the two varieties swap genotypes.
Height in corn is set by the environment alone, so the genotype of the plant has no effect.

items.q: Select the examples of phenotypic plasticity.
options: An arrowhead plant grows ribbon-like leaves under water and arrow-shaped leaves in air.
Water fleas grow longer spines when they detect chemicals released by predatory insects.
Two pink snapdragons produce red, pink and white offspring in a 1:2:1 ratio.
A four o'clock plant's seedlings have the leaf color of the branch that gave the eggs.
A testcross of a double heterozygote gives four classes of offspring in equal numbers.

items.q: Put the steps that turn a hydrangea's flowers blue in order.
options: The soil is acidic (low pH).
Aluminum in the soil dissolves.
The roots take up the dissolved aluminum.
Aluminum reaches the flowers and binds the pigment.
The flowers look blue.

items.q: Yarrow plants from the coast are taller than yarrow plants from the mountains. Which result would best show that the difference is at least partly genetic?
options: Clones of both kinds grown together in one garden still differ in height.
Coastal plants are taller in each coastal population that researchers have measured.
Mountain plants grown in the mountains stay short for several years in a row.
Coastal soil contains more nitrogen than the soil in the mountain habitats.

items.q: A gardener's hydrangea had blue flowers in acidic soil. After she adds lime, which raises the soil pH, it blooms pink. She plants its seeds in acidic soil. Predict the flower color of the seedlings, assuming they inherited alleles for colored flowers.
options: Blue, because the lime changed the parent's phenotype but not the alleles in its seeds.
Pink, because the parent plant was blooming pink at the time its seeds were made.
A 3:1 ratio of pink to blue, because pink has now become the dominant color.
White, because the change in soil pH damaged the parent's alleles for flower color.
